Where the learned manifold fails

Clipping helps. Most remaining error is inaccurate coverage along the stroke’s edges.

How much error does clipping remove?

ModelRaw captureClipped captureSquared error removedClipped pixel RMS

Same 16,384 additional uniform images for both models. Each is 784 coverage values: 0 is no ink, 1 is full ink, and intermediate values are legitimate partially covered pixels. Capture compares squared error with squared distance to this cloud’s mean.

Clipping removes impossible values. It still permits a stroke with wrong edge coverage, width, tilt, caps, or geometry.

The old magenta overlay deliberately makes tiny violations conspicuous: a value only 0.000001 beyond a bound receives about 10% magenta tint. The grayscale display already clamps raw values. A pink patch is a diagnostic flag, rather than an equivalent amount of visible ink.

Connected artifacts versus disconnected ink

ModelBounds-violating pixels / imageConnected to stroke regionDisconnected ink pixels / imageImages with an islandIsland share of clipped error

Connectivity uses eight neighboring pixels. A bounds anomaly is connected through reference ink plus anomaly pixels; negative values are counted as anomalies, not actual ink. After clipping, foreground is coverage greater than the selected cutoff. Its main component has the largest overlap with actual stroke ink. Counts are pooled over images; threshold changes can break faint bridges.

Inspect the actual pixel errors

Stored manifold nodes are full pixel vectors. Because cell weights are nonnegative and sum to one, bounded nodes guarantee bounded interpolation (up to roundoff). Clamping already-fitted nodes is a different operation from fitting under bounds; it can destroy cancellations that currently improve in-range pixels.

Is it the wrong knob setting, or an invalid stroke shape?

This diagnostic fits the original renderer to a clipped reconstruction using bounded nonlinear least squares and two initial guesses. It changes no learned model. The fit is an upper bound on exact nearest-family distance, with no global minimum proof. Red in the last panel means excess ink relative to the valid fit; blue means missing ink; fixed scale ±0.2. Some large selected errors mostly resemble a valid stroke with a wrong height; typical interior errors mostly persist after adjusting knobs.

Does a learned direction match an actual knob change?

A direction is a change value in each of the 784 pixel dimensions. A small wrong component changes a pixel that should stay fixed. There is also a stricter constraint: legitimate knob changes produce coupled edge changes, not arbitrary independent pixel changes.

Physical knobBest corresponding learned axisBest combination of five axes10%-range move: calibrated direction10%-range move: reconstructed endpoints

Every number is direction-error L2 divided by actual direction L2, expressed as a percentage; smaller is better. These are not percentages of image variance. Local tangent tests use 128 interior images and central differences of 0.1% of each knob range. Values in this table use clipping.

Mixing learned coordinates helps, so a single initialized axis is an imperfect physical knob. Error remaining after the best combination measures directions that the learned local surface still cannot reproduce. Tangent-normal residuals can include curvature as well as invalid pixel patterns.

How much do coordinates need to mix?
Learned coordinatecxcyheightwidthlean

Median absolute entries of local calibration G, where learned pixel Jacobian × G best approximates actual knob Jacobian. Both coordinates and knobs use fractions of their ranges. Columns are physical knob changes; rows are learned-coordinate changes. Off-diagonal entries are chart mixing, not automatically pixel leakage. Calibration varies with the starting image.

See a real knob move and its learned pixel vector

Locally calibrated transport uses the actual physical tangent at the starting point to choose the best combination of learned directions, then holds that calibration fixed during the finite move. This is an optimistic diagnostic; the current model does not provide a learned physical knob controller. Separately reconstructed endpoints also see both true images, so that comparison tests representation quality rather than prediction from a knob alone.

What the evidence suggests fixing

  1. Keep output clipping as a clear, measured correction for impossible values. Its error reduction is real, and its limits are visible above.
  2. Fit under pixel bounds rather than clamp already-fitted nodes. Test the tradeoff between physical bounds, smoothing, and reconstruction accuracy.
  3. Target cap and boundary accuracy, especially height and vertical position. The selected large failures hit learned-coordinate bounds and barely improve with broader projection. Test stronger coverage of boundary faces, adaptive grids, and a penalty on errors in actual small knob-change vectors.
  4. Track valid shape and direction errors alongside variance capture. A connected, bounded image can still lie outside the generated stroke family.

There is no injected random noise in the learned decoder. The residuals are deterministic for fixed coordinates. Their concentration on stroke boundaries and their repeatable direction mismatch are structured errors; these diagnostics do not prove a unique causal contribution from smoothing, grid resolution, or coordinate projection.

How much fitting effort did it take?

The comparison follows the winning refinement paths. Times are read from prior fitting-loop logs and exclude initialization overhead, sampling, diagnostic projections, and discarded attempts. Grid and curve iterations perform different amounts of work. The uniform 5D grid alone remained below the best curves; useful knob-informed allocation mattered.
